approachQuestion.prompt:
Dispatch batches

A lowercase string lists parcel types in arrival order. Cut it into as many nonempty contiguous batches as possible, subject to every letter appearing in at most one batch across the whole dispatch. Return only the maximum batch count.

Example 1: s="abacdecd" → 2, batches "aba" and "cdecd".
Example 2: s="abc" → 3.
Example 3: s="" → 0.

Constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; alphabet is exactly the 26 lowercase English letters. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: In a first scan store the last index of each of the 26 letters in a fixed array. In a second scan maintain end as the greatest last index of a letter seen in the current batch. Close the batch whenever the current index equals end.
options.feedback: Once a letter enters a batch, all its later occurrences must enter that batch too. The maximum last occurrence is therefore a forced boundary. Closing at that first safe boundary leaves the most opportunities for later batches.

options.text: Close a batch immediately before any letter that has not appeared earlier in the string.
options.feedback: The new letter may be followed by a letter from an earlier batch. For "aba", cutting before b separates the two a occurrences and is illegal.

options.text: Return the number of distinct letters.
options.feedback: Different letters can be forced into one batch by interleaving occurrences. For "abab", there are two letters but only one valid batch.

options.text: Use the same two scans and batch boundaries, but store each position’s running end in a separate length-n array before counting boundaries.
options.feedback: The forced boundary rule remains correct. However, each running end is used only to test the current position; the length-n history can be replaced by one scalar.

A batch cannot close before the last occurrence of any letter already inside it. Extend its frontier as new letters appear; close at the first index reaching that frontier to maximize the number of batches.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method with the 26-entry last-index array, two iterative scans and scalar counters. The alphabet size is a fixed constant, not an input parameter. No input copy, dynamic map or recursion is used. Let n=len(s). Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

feedback.reason: Two scans use one fixed 26-entry last-position array.

messages.text: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
The scans do not restart for each item.
In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.

details: The two scans take O(n) worst-case time. The 26-entry array is fixed-size and all other state is scalar, so auxiliary space is O(1). The input and scalar output are excluded; there is no hashing or recursion.
Fixed alphabet of 26 letters; fixed last-index array; two iterative scans.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n)”: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(1)”: The scans do not restart for each item.
“Time O(1), auxiliary space O(1)”: In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.
